<reason>Both sides were sharp, but PRO (B) held the decisive frame — honoring versus remembering — and answered the two hardest attacks on it. CON's best weapons were the line-drawing problem (the Colston "what was the honor for?" trap) and the form/context dilemma ("either context defeats bronze, so annotate in place, or it doesn't, so relocation is theatre"). PRO neutralized the second cleanly and memorably with the frame argument: the square speaks in the city's voice, funded and renewed daily, while the museum speaks in the voice of evidence — nobody reads a Klan robe in a vitrine as endorsement, so "the building already won." That resolved the dilemma rather than dodging it. On Colston, PRO's answer ("the almshouses were the trade's proceeds; the honor rests on the money and the money was the trade") plus the closing contrast ("Colston's charity was the trade's proceeds; Washington's marble is for founding a republic") held up better than CON's rejoinder that Washington's fortune also rested on slavery, since Washington's monuments are not raised for his wealth. PRO also turned CON's own signature remedy against it: carving the names of the enslaved at the enslaver's base stages the hierarchy permanently — owner aloft, owned underfoot — and CON quietly retreated from that proposal to an equal-scale counter-figure that PRO plausibly showed councils will never fund, making CON's "interim" the permanent enslaver-aloft outcome. CON's Q2 answer honestly refused to put Colston back on the plinth, which is candid but concedes the paradigm application of the motion while CON's remaining objection narrows to "make it a local argument, not a category rule." That reframe is genuinely interesting and PRO under-exploited it, but PRO's closing weighing ("argue the middle cases forever; the cost of a borderline error falls on a dead man's reputation, the cost of CON's error falls every morning on the child") gave the cleaner decision rule. Execution also matters: CON had two turns clipped for exceeding the cap, including the second rebuttal cut off exactly at its answer to the frame point, so its resolution of the central clash never arrived.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's turn on CON's own proposal — carving the names of the enslaved into their enslaver's plinth "stages the hierarchy in permanent form, the owner still aloft, the owned still underfoot" — plus the frame answer to CON's form/context dilemma ("the wall label isn't fighting the bronze; the building already won"), which together forced CON to abandon its headline remedy for an unfunded counter-monument.</best_rebuttal>
